docs.description: Case name: Kelly v. Robinson Opinion filed: 1986-11-12 Docket No.: 85-1033 Citations: • 93 L. Ed. 2d 216 • 107 S. Ct. 353 • 479 U.S. 36 • 1986 U.S. LEXIS 17 Case holding summaries: • stating that a law's "object and policy" should be considered when construing a statute • giving weight to pre-Code practice that was "widely accepted" and "established" • stating that a single sentence or member of a sentence should not control the endeavor of expounding statutes • "we must ... look to the provisions of the whole law" • Powell, J., joined by Rehnquist, C.J., and Brennan, White, Blackmun, O'Connor, and Scalia, JJ. • "Although restitution does resemble a judgment `for the benefit of' the victim, the context in which it is imposed undermines that conclusion. The victim has no control over ... the decision to award restitution." • restitution obligations made condition of probation in state criminal conviction nondischargeable • "if Congress intends for legislation to change the interpretation of a judicially created concept, it makes that intent specific" • prospect of federal remission of judgments in some cases "would hamper the flexibility of state criminal judges in choosing the combination of imprisonment, fines, and restitution most likely to further the rehabilitative and deterrent goals of state criminal justice systems" (emphasis added) • holding that "the `starting point in every case involving construction of a statute is the language itself'" (quoting Blue Chip Stamps v. Manor Drug Stores, 421 U.S. 723, 756, 95 S.Ct. 1917, 44 L.Ed.2d 539 (1975) (Powell, J., concurring)) • the Code's definition of "debt" is broadly crafted; other Code provisions and legislative history all support a broad reading of the definition • "The starting point in every case involving construction of a statute is the language itself." • criminal restitution obligations were a "fine, penalty, or forfeiture" under Section 523(a)(7) of the Bankruptcy Code because (1 • criminal restitution obligations were a "fine, penalty, or forfeiture" under Section 523(a)(7) of the Bankruptcy Code because (1) criminal restitution is not merely concerned with benefiting victims but also with punishing and rehabilitating the offender, (2 • statutes should not be read "`with the ease of a computer'" • in inter- preting a statute, a court “must not be guided by a single sentence or member of a sentence, but look to the provi- sions of the whole law, and to its object and policy” (inter- nal quotation marks omitted) • Making restitution orders dischargeable "would hamper the flexibility of state criminal judges in choosing the combination of imprisonment, fines, and restitution most likely to further the rehabilitative and deterrent goals of state criminal justice systems." • “[T]he direct relation between the harm and the punishment gives restitution a more precise deterrent effect than a traditional fine.” • giving weight to pre-Code practice that was "widely accepted" and "established" • comments made at hearings, which were not statements of Congressional members and were not included in the official reports, are insignificant in determining legislative intent • "We acknowledge that a few comments in the hearings ... may suggest that the language bears the interpretation.... We decline to accord any significance to these statements." • in construing statute, court must look not at a single sentence but at the provisions of the entire statute • holding that criminal restitution orders fall within the meaning of § 523(a)(7) • "we must consider the [Code's] language ... in light of the history of bankruptcy court deference to criminal judgments and in light of the interests of the States in unfettered administration of their criminal justice systems" • restitution imposed as a condition of probation in state criminal proceedings was excepted from Chapter 7 discharge • "We acknowledge that a few comments in the hearings ... may suggest that the language bears the interpretation.... We decline to accord any significance to these statements." • statutes should not be read "`with the ease of a computer'" • “In expounding a statute, we must not be guided by a single sentence or member of a sentence, but look to the provisions of the whole law, and to its object and policy.” (quoting Offshore Logistics, Inc. v. Tallentire, 477 U.S. 207, 222 (1986)) • holding that restitution obligations imposed as conditions of probation in state criminal proceedings are not dischargeable in Chapter 7 bankruptcy because they are primarily penal rather than compensatory • "The starting point in every case involving construction of a statute is the language itself." • predicating the result in Kelly on “the strong interests of the States, the uniform construction of the old [Bankruptcy] Act over three-quarters of a century, and the absence of any significant evidence that Congress intended to change the law in this area” • holding that debt for criminal restitution is nondischargeable pursuant to § 523(a)(7) • holding that criminal restitution obligations constitute a "fine, penalty, or forfeiture" under § 523(a) of the Bankruptcy Code • "[R]estitution is forwarded to the victim, and may be calculated by reference to the amount of harm the offender has caused." • describing restitution imposed as part of a state probationary criminal sentence as a “penalty” that could not be discharged in bankruptcy proceedings • "In expounding a statute, we must not be guided by a single sentence or member of a sentence, but look to the provisions of the whole law, and to its object and policy." • noting that “Congress enacted the Code in 1978 against the background of an established judicial exception . . . created in the face of a statute drafted with considerable care and specificity” and finding no “significant evidence that Congress intended to change the law” • determining that criminal penalties under the Act were non-dischargeable • giving weight to pre-Code practice that was “widely accepted” and “established” • criminal restitution obligation was not dischargeable • state need not appear and enter an objection to the discharge to defend state criminal judgment before a federal bankruptcy court • holding that restitution obligations imposed as a condition of probation by a state court are nondischargeable within § 523(a)(7) • entertaining without comment the affirmative defense of discharge in bankruptcy • “[T]he States’ interest in administering their criminal justice systems free from federal interference is one of the most powerful of the considerations that should influence a court considering equitable types of relief.” • "federal bankruptcy courts should not invalidate the results of state criminal proceedings" • expressing "serious doubts" as to whether restitution orders are ever dischargeable • recognizing that S 523(a)(7)"codified the judicially created exception to discharge for fines [, penalties and forfeitures]" • definition of "debt" broadly drafted • holding “a criminal judgment that takes the form of restitution” is within “the penal goals of the State” and is nondischargeable • order of restitution entered as condition or probation not dischargeable in Chapter 7 bankruptcy proceeding
